---
title: Evaluation
description: "Measure whether the model finds more disputes at the team's review capacity, and compare each addition fairly."
---

Suppose the risk team from the payment tutorials can investigate a fixed
number of payments in each review period. Use a held-out dataset of past
review decisions, model scores, and settled dispute labels to ask whether
the ranking would have found more later disputes at that capacity.
Assess that decision alongside validation loss before adding profile fields
or another task. With several targets, an improving combined loss can hide
a regression in an individual outcome.

## Measure the review decision

Choose the same eligible payments and review cutoff for every model. For
the first comparison, use the latest payment from each account-review
observation: the flat model scores that payment, and the history model's
last transaction result scores the same payment with more context. Keep
the settled dispute labels and 30-day outcome windows identical.

For each review period, rank those payments by score and select the number
the team can investigate. **Precision** is the fraction of reviewed payments
that later receive disputes. **Recall** is the fraction of all later disputes
among the eligible payments that the review found. Higher recall at the same
review capacity means the ranking found more of those disputes.

Here `scored_payments` is an application-supplied collection of records for
one review period, each with `payment_id`, settled Boolean `disputed`, and
the model's `probability`. `review_capacity` is the team's maximum payment
count for that period:

```python
ranked = sorted(scored_payments, key=lambda payment: payment["probability"], reverse=True)
reviewed = ranked[:review_capacity]
found = sum(payment["disputed"] for payment in reviewed)
total = sum(payment["disputed"] for payment in ranked)
precision = found / len(reviewed) if reviewed else float("nan")
recall = found / total if total else float("nan")
```

Use the same periods, capacities, and tie handling for each model. Aggregate
the counts across periods before computing overall precision and recall.
If the application instead uses a probability threshold, it may select a
different number of payments each period. Choose that policy on validation
data, then assess the fixed choice on test data.

## Read the metrics

Here `model` is the fitted history model from
[Train and save](train-and-save.qmd). The validation file contains separate
account-review rows with the same `trxns` structure and settled labels:

```python
import relflow as rf

validation_data = rf.ArrowDataModule(validate="payments/history/validation.parquet")
metrics = model.validate(validation_data, batch_size=256)
validation_loss = metrics[0]["loss/validate"]
dispute_auc = metrics[0][".trxns.disputed/validate.auc.content"]
```

Loss measures the model's target-prediction error; lower is better for the
same objectives and observations. relflow calls this reconstruction loss
because it predicts hidden values, including the supervised dispute labels.
AUC measures how well scores rank disputed payments above undisputed ones
across thresholds; higher is better, with 0.5 indicating chance ranking.
It does not measure recall at a particular review capacity.

The history model's built-in dispute metrics pool **every retained
transaction target**, including earlier transactions. The flat model has
one target per row. Compare these models on the same latest-payment scores
as above; their default pooled AUCs describe different target populations.
If the application reviews all historical transactions, instead prepare
matching flat-model observations and outcomes for that same population.
For a controlled test of history inputs alone, also match the training
target population and target weighting.

Set the evaluation batch size on the method call; see
[Batch size](../guides/training-options.qmd#batch-size) for its persistent model setting and
per-device meaning.

relflow uses Lightning's native logging. Attached loggers receive training
metrics only at the configured step cadence, every `log_every_n_steps` optimizer
updates. Validation and test losses and content metrics summarize each pass.
Throughput is logged per step. Each tensorfield determines which content
metrics are available. [Training options](../guides/training-options.qmd#report-progress-and-validate)
explains how logging, validation, and checkpoint schedules are configured.

| Metric | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| `loss/train` | Training loss from the latest batch: the sum of active leaf losses after each leaf's `weight` is applied. |
| `loss/train_epoch` | Internal training loss average for callbacks; not sent to attached loggers. |
| `loss/validate`, `loss/test` | Aggregate reconstruction loss for each evaluation pass. |
| `.trxns.disputed/validate.loss.state` | Reconstruction loss for dispute value states at `/trxns/disputed`. |
| `.trxns.disputed/validate.loss.content` | Datatype-specific content loss across transaction dispute labels. |
| `.trxns.disputed/validate.auc.content` | Example Boolean content metric over the retained transactions. |
| `throughput/train` | Observations processed per second per rank for the latest batch, using its actual row count and reported at the configured step logging cadence. |
| `throughput/validate`, `throughput/test`, `throughput/predict` | Observations processed per second per rank for each evaluation or prediction batch, using its actual row count. |

Metric names join schema-address components with periods, preserve case,
and prefix the address group with a period before appending `/stage.metric.component`.
For example, `/trxns/disputed` becomes `.trxns.disputed/validate.auc.content`.
The leading period distinguishes address groups from aggregate groups
such as `loss` and `throughput`. The root uses `.`, as in `./validate.loss.state`.
A leaf can contribute both state and content loss. State metrics describe valued, null, padded,
masked, and other states; content metrics describe the value being predicted.
Leaf metrics are logged before weighting, so their unweighted sum need not
match the total loss.

If no reconstruction coordinate is selected anywhere across distributed ranks,
the training batch is skipped. Validation/test return zero loss for that
batch. Repeated empty-objective warnings suggest a mismatch among masks,
source geometry, and split contents; they do not demonstrate learning.

## Check probability calibration {#check-probability-calibration}

A useful ranking can still give inaccurate probability estimates.
Calibration asks whether, for example, payments assigned probabilities near
0.1 actually receive disputes about 10% of the time. Group held-out scores
into ranges and compare their average probabilities with their observed
dispute rates. Boolean training uses frequency-weighted loss, so the raw
probability output alone does not establish calibration.

Fit any calibration adjustment on a separate held-out calibration split,
and evaluate the adjusted scores on test data. Use the same eligible
payment population and outcome window as the review comparison.

## Numeric targets and missing values

For a numeric target such as the later
[account-loss outcome](nested-context-and-account-outcomes.qmd), Number content loss and error
metrics include selected reconstruction coordinates only when the true value
is `valued`. Null outcomes still teach the state objective, but do not act as
numeric zero targets. Validation/test MAE and RMSE accumulate error totals and
valued-target counts across the full pass and distributed ranks. For example,
one eligible target in a batch has one tenth the weight of ten targets in
another batch. RMSE takes its square root after the squared errors have been
combined; it is not an average of batch RMSEs. See [Number](../datatypes/number.qmd).

Compare candidate models on the same source and eligible coordinates before
setting early-stopping thresholds.
Loss aggregation remains separate from the target-counted content metrics.

## Compare models fairly

Use the same held-out observations, target definitions, preprocessing, and
masking policy across comparisons. Keep entity groups and time boundaries
consistent with deployment; construct those splits before supplying them to
the [data module](../guides/data-modules.qmd).

Choose an output-specific metric alongside `loss/validate`. Number errors and
categorical accuracy measure different things; their scale and eligible
coordinates differ. A state-accuracy improvement alone does not establish
better content predictions. Use validation data to choose thresholds and
checkpoints, leaving the test split for a final assessment.

Hash validation uses fixed salt zero, matching test and prediction; training
still resalts each batch. Keep this encoding policy consistent when comparing
validation scores. If using
[EMA](../guides/checkpoints-ema-and-resuming.qmd#average-learned-parameters-with-ema), validation and checkpoint
selection during fit use the averaged parameters. Record that choice alongside
the architecture and dataset split.

Evaluate the additions in the same order as the examples. Change one modeling
choice at a time:

| Question | Comparison |
| --- | --- |
| Does the history help? | Compare the payment-only model, the history model, and a tuned tabular baseline with spending counts, totals, and recency on the same latest-payment decisions. |
| Do richer transaction and profile fields help? | Add payment channel and account tenure to the same history model. |
| Do shared outcomes help? | Compare the joint dispute/repeat model with a separate model for each task, inspecting each outcome's metric. |
| Does deeper account context help? | Add purchase line items, then the separate withdrawal history in the [account example](nested-context-and-account-outcomes.qmd), keeping the same transaction-level targets. |
| Does pretraining help? | Compare fine-tuning with the same supervised architecture trained from scratch. |
| Is the representation reusable? | Keep the exporting model fixed and compare downstream predictors using existing features, exported vectors, and both together. |

Keep the prediction time and future outcome window identical across these
comparisons. A payment without a recorded dispute yet may still be awaiting
its outcome; define when a negative label is ready before building the splits.
See [Customer outcomes](../use-cases/customer-outcomes.qmd) for concrete
entity, history, and outcome-window definitions.

Preserving individual events has a cost: more preparation, retained records,
and model computation. Choose that representation when its task improvement
justifies those costs. A good aggregate-feature model remains a useful option
and a necessary comparison.

Record the generated architecture and capacity preset with each result.
Changing the schema can change both the available context and the model's
size. Measure training cost and serving latency for the actual record
lengths and hardware alongside predictive quality. A result on one dataset
does not establish the same advantage for another task or a reused embedding.

Boolean fields accept one threshold or a list of thresholds for metrics.
When constructing the model, replace the `disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True)`
field inside `trxns` with this declaration:

```python
disputed=rf.Boolean(
    mask=True,
    threshold=[0.5, 0.7, 0.9],
)
```

This changes threshold-qualified accuracy, precision, recall, and specificity
metrics. It does not change the training loss or the probability-only
prediction payload. Category `topk` likewise adds datatype-specific metrics;
see the relevant [datatype reference](../datatypes/index.qmd).

## Measure dependence on an input

An ablation temporarily removes an input and reevaluates the trained model.
For example, removing amount evidence from every transaction, including the
latest, measures how the same model performs without those values. Compare
the target's task metric as well as total loss. Missing-input
behavior can be out of distribution for a model that never saw such absence;
training with suitable structural dropout can make the comparison more useful.
An ablation shows dependence under this experiment, not causation.

[Schema mutation](../guides/schema-mutation.qmd) shows how to select inputs and
temporarily override their settings, including what is restored afterward.

The [modeling evidence](../evidence.qmd) give worked examples of held-out
metrics, corrupted-input controls, and deliberately lossy representations.
Each scenario includes its model tree and the current evidence for its claim.
